propositions.text: Whether retrospective changes to sentence conditions can constitute 'punishment' violating s. 11(h) of the Charter.
propositions.quote: This Court must decide whether retrospective changes to the conditions of a sentence may in some circumstances constitute “punishment” in violation of the s. 11 (h) right not to be punished twice for the same offence.

propositions.text: Distinction between sentence imposed and conditions of sentence in criminal law.
propositions.quote: The criminal law distinguishes between the sentence imposed on an offender and the conditions of the sentence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue whether retrospective changes to sentence conditions violate s. 11(h) and notes the legal distinction between sentence and conditions.

propositions.text: The appeal arises from Parliament's conclusion that APR was ineffective, established in 1992 legislation.
propositions.quote: This appeal results from Parliament’s conclusion that accelerated parole review, or APR, was not working.

propositions.text: APR allowed first-time non-violent offenders parole consideration based on a single question about violent offence risk.
propositions.quote: APR was a simplified process that allowed first-time non-violent offenders to be considered for parole on the basis of a single question: Are there no reasonable grounds to believe that the offender, if released, is likely to commit a violent offence?

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appeal arises from Parliament's view that APR was ineffective, describing APR's simplified parole review process.

propositions.text: Crown cites criticism of APR from inception, including concerns about violent recidivism test's reliability.
propositions.quote: The Crown cites criticism of APR that dated back to its inception. Even before the legislation establishing APR was enacted, the Canadian Criminal Justice Association had expressed concerns about the violent recidivism test.

propositions.text: Canadian Criminal Justice Association argued APR would allow offenders with violent records to qualify.
propositions.quote: It argued that APR would be available to some offenders who “have records with previous incarceration in Provincial institutions for offences including those of violence”

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues APR was criticized from the start for its violent recidivism test and allowing offenders with violent records to qualify.

propositions.text: Despite criticism, APR was expanded in 1997 to include earlier eligibility for day parole.
propositions.quote: Despite this and other criticism, the APR process was expanded in 1997 to include earlier eligibility for day parole

paragraphs.summary: The court notes APR was expanded in 1997 to allow earlier day parole eligibility despite criticism.

propositions.text: Crown notes continued criticism recommending tightening APR eligibility and changing recidivism criteria.
propositions.quote: The Crown notes that criticism continued to be levelled at APR in the ensuing years. ... recommended “tightening the eligibility criteria” for APR ... and “changing the risk of recidivism criterion”

paragraphs.summary: The Crown notes ongoing criticism recommending stricter APR eligibility and altered recidivism criteria.

propositions.text: 2007 Correctional Service Review Panel concluded statutory and accelerated parole undermined discretionary release and were less effective.
propositions.quote: In a 2007 report, the Correctional Service of Canada Review Panel concluded that “statutory release and accelerated parole have both undermined discretionary release and generally have not proved as effective as discretionary release in mitigating violent reoffending”

paragraphs.summary: The Crown cites a 2007 report concluding statutory and accelerated parole undermined discretionary release and were less effective.

propositions.text: Parliament repealed APR provisions in 2011 via AEPA, which applied retrospectively.
propositions.quote: Parliament repealed the relevant provisions. The Abolition of Early Parole Act ... eliminated APR ... by virtue of s. 10(1) of the AEPA , the repeal applied retrospectively.

propositions.text: Respondents were convicted of serious non-violent crimes when APR was in effect and would have been eligible for early day parole.
propositions.quote: Mr. Whaling, Ms. Slobbe and Mr. Maidana had all been convicted of serious, but non-violent, crimes at a time when APR remained in effect. Each of them would have been eligible for early day parole under the repealed provisions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Parliament repealed APR retrospectively, affecting respondents convicted when APR was in effect and eligible for early day parole.

propositions.text: Whether retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violates respondents' s. 11(h) Charter right not to be punished twice.
propositions.quote: The question before this Court is whether the retrospective application of the delayed eligibility for day parole ... violated the respondents’ right, guaranteed by s. 11 (h) of the Charter , not to be punished anew for their offences.

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issue whether retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violates respondents' s. 11(h) right.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) applies to respondents' claim; retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violated s. 11(h) right and was not justified under s. 1.
propositions.quote: I find that s. 11 (h) applies to the respondents’ claim. The retrospective application of delayed day parole eligibility violated the respondents’ s. 11 (h) right not to be “punished . . . again”, and that violation was not justified under s. 1 of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 11(h) applies and retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violated respondents' rights, unjustified under s. 1.

propositions.text: No need to address respondents' s. 7 Charter claim after finding s. 11(h) violation.
propositions.quote: Having found that the specific right enshrined in s. 11 (h) was violated, I do not find it necessary to address the respondents’ claim with respect to the more general right guaranteed by s. 7 of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The court declines to address respondents' s. 7 claim after finding s. 11(h) violation.

propositions.text: Appeal from BC Court of Appeal decision upholding BC Supreme Court summary trial decision in respondents' favour.
propositions.quote: This is an appeal from a decision in which the British Columbia Court of Appeal upheld a summary trial decision of the British Columbia Supreme Court. Both courts found in the respondents’ favour.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the appeal is from BC Court of Appeal upholding BC Supreme Court decision favoring respondents.

propositions.text: Respondents were serving federal sentences and were eligible for APR as first-time non-violent offenders at sentencing.
propositions.quote: The respondents, Mr. Whaling, Ms. Slobbe and Mr. Maidana, were all serving federal penitentiary sentences. As first-time, non-violent offenders, all three were eligible for APR under the system in place at the time of their sentencing

paragraphs.summary: The court states respondents were serving federal sentences and eligible for APR at sentencing.

propositions.text: APR was automatic, paper-based, with a lower parole release test and no discretion to deny if test met.
propositions.quote: APR was different from normal parole review in a few ways. First, the process was simplified. The APR application was automatic ... The review was conducted on paper, without a hearing ... the Board had no discretion to decide against releasing the offender

paragraphs.summary: The court describes APR as automatic, paper-based, with a lower parole release test and no discretion to deny release if test met.

propositions.text: From 1997, APR day parole eligibility triggered earlier: after one sixth of sentence or six months, whichever longer.
propositions.quote: beginning in 1997, the APR process for day parole was triggered at an earlier date than in the normal process: after the offender had served one sixth of the sentence or six months (whichever was longer)

paragraphs.summary: The court states that from 1997 APR day parole eligibility was triggered earlier than normal parole.

propositions.text: AEPA repealed APR provisions and applied repeal retrospectively to offenders sentenced before repeal.
propositions.quote: Sections 3 and 5 of the AEPA repealed the CCRA ’s APR provisions ... while s. 10(1) of the AEPA made the abolition of APR apply retrospectively to offenders already serving their sentences.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) of AEPA states APR does not apply to offenders sentenced before or after repeal date.
propositions.quote: 10. (1) Subject to subsection (2), the accelerated parole review process ... does not apply, as of that day, to offenders who were sentenced ... before, on or after the day of that coming into force.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains AEPA repealed APR provisions and applied repeal retrospectively to all offenders sentenced before or after repeal.

propositions.text: APR repeal replaced earlier day parole eligibility with normal parole timing and changed review process and parole test.
propositions.quote: Instead of APR, the normal parole provisions ... would now apply. This changed the timing of eligibility for day parole ... It also changed the review process ... and the test for granting parole ... reverted to the more onerous one of “undue risk to society”

paragraphs.summary: The court details how APR repeal replaced earlier day parole eligibility with normal timing, changed review process, and parole test.

propositions.text: Repeal delayed day parole eligibility for respondents by 3, 9, and 21 months respectively.
propositions.quote: The immediate effect of the repeal was to delay the day parole eligibility dates of all three respondents: Mr. Whaling’s by three months, Ms. Slobbe’s by nine months, and Mr. Maidana’s by twenty-one months.

paragraphs.summary: The court states repeal delayed respondents' day parole eligibility by 3, 9, and 21 months respectively.

propositions.text: Respondents challenged constitutionality of s. 10(1) AEPA by summary trial in BC Supreme Court.
propositions.quote: The respondents challenged the constitutionality of s. 10(1) of the AEPA by way of a summary trial in the British Columbia Supreme Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes respondents challenged s. 10(1) AEPA constitutionality by summary trial in BC Supreme Court.

propositions.text: Holmes J. held s. 10(1) AEPA infringed s. 11(h) as additional punishment and was not justified under s. 1.
propositions.quote: Holmes J., the summary trial judge, held that s. 10(1) of the AEPA infringed s. 11 (h) of the Charter because it amounted to additional punishment, and that it was not saved under s. 1 of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker held s. 10(1) AEPA infringed s. 11(h) and was not justified under s. 1.

propositions.text: Holmes J. reasoned s. 11(h) protects against additional punishment after conviction, relying on R. v. Rodgers.
propositions.quote: Holmes J. began by asking whether the abolition of APR amounted to punishment in violation of the respondents’ right under s. 11 (h) of the Charter ... She reasoned on the basis of R. v. Rodgers ... that “[s.] 11(h)’s protections carry on past trial, conviction (or acquittal), and sentence, to prevent any additional trial or punishment for the offence with which the person was once charged”

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reasoned s. 11(h) protects against additional punishment after conviction, citing R. v. Rodgers.

propositions.text: Punishment occurs when a consequence is part of sanctions for an offence and furthers sentencing principles.
propositions.quote: As a general rule, it seems to me that the consequence will constitute a punishment when it forms part of the arsenal of sanctions to which an accused may be liable in respect of a particular offence and the sanction is one imposed in furtherance of the purpose and principles of sentencing.

propositions.text: Delayed parole eligibility is punishment in criminal sentencing context.
propositions.quote: She pointed out that delayed parole eligibility is clearly used as “punishment” in the context of criminal sentencing, citing several decisions of this Court

propositions.text: Parole ineligibility from retrospective CCRA amendment is not materially different from parole ineligibility imposed as part of sentence.
propositions.quote: parole ineligibility imposed as part of a sentence under the Criminal Code ... is not materially different from parole ineligibility resulting from the retrospective amendment of the CCRA

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found delayed parole eligibility is punishment and retrospective parole ineligibility is similar to sentencing parole ineligibility.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) of AEPA has punitive purposes and retrospective alteration of day parole eligibility is punitive in effect.
propositions.quote: Holmes J. found that there was “abundant evidence” that its purposes were punitive in nature ... the effect of the retrospective alteration of day parole eligibility was punitive

propositions.text: Retrospective parole eligibility alteration significantly affects how offenders serve sentences.
propositions.quote: this alteration would have a “significant actual effect on the way in which the two offenders who are still in prison will serve their sentences”

propositions.text: Changes to parole law that significantly limit parole eligibility of already sentenced offenders constitute additional punishment.
propositions.quote: such changes do not include significant limitations ... to the parole eligibility of offenders who have already been sentenced ... A change that includes such limitations occasions additional punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found s.10(1) AEPA punitive in purpose and effect, significantly limiting parole eligibility as additional punishment.

propositions.text: Infringement of s.11(h) was established and not saved under s.1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: Having established an infringement of s. 11 (h), Holmes J. found that the infringement was not saved under s. 1 of the Charter

propositions.text: Objectives of retrospective repeal included maintaining public confidence but impairment was not minimal.
propositions.quote: the objectives underlying the retrospective application of the repeal ... were pressing and substantial, the Attorney General ... had not shown that the provision impaired the respondents’ s. 11 (h) rights no more than was necessary

propositions.text: Section 10(1) declared invalid to extent it applies retrospectively to offenders sentenced before March 28, 2011, with immediate effect.
propositions.quote: Holmes J. declared s. 10(1) to be invalid to the extent that it made the AEPA apply retrospectively ... The declaration was to have immediate effect.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found s.10(1) infringed s.11(h) and was invalid retrospectively with immediate effect.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal upheld trial judge's decision with some reasoning variations.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge’s decision, although with a few variations in reasoning.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) protects against double jeopardy including sanctions imposed after sentencing.
propositions.quote: Levine J.A., writing for the court, found that the purpose of s. 11 (h) is to protect against double jeopardy

propositions.text: Retrospective legislative lengthening of jail time by delaying parole eligibility violated s.11(h).
propositions.quote: the retrospective legislative lengthening of the time the respondents would spend in jail ... violated their right under s. 11 (h) not to be “punished again”

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge, finding retrospective parole delay violated s.11(h) protection against double jeopardy.

propositions.text: Distinction between sentencing judge and Board roles does not alter conclusion that s.10(1) AEPA is punishment.
propositions.quote: Levine J.A. emphasized the distinction ... This did not alter her conclusion that s. 10(1) of the AEPA nonetheless amounted to punishment

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found s.10(1) AEPA punitive despite role distinctions between judge and Board.

propositions.text: Overly narrow reading of s.11(h) is contrary to Charter interpretation principles.
propositions.quote: Levine J.A. noted that an overly narrow reading of s. 11 (h) is contrary to the appropriate principles of Charter interpretation.

propositions.text: Issue is meaning of 'punishment' for s.11(h) purposes, focusing on sanctions and sentencing principles per Rodgers.
propositions.quote: The issue was the meaning of “punishment” for the purposes of s. 11 (h), and this turned on whether the consequence in this case “forms part of the arsenal of [possible] sanctions” and furthers the “purpose and principles of sentencing”, as required by Rodgers

propositions.text: Effect of delayed parole eligibility by legislation is analogous to judge-imposed delayed parole eligibility, thus violating s.11(h).
propositions.quote: she held that the effect of the delayed parole eligibility imposed by way of legislation was analogous to that of delayed parole eligibility imposed by a judge

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found s.10(1) AEPA punitive in effect, violating s.11(h), and rejected overly narrow interpretation of 'punishment'.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal agreed legislation was enacted for pressing concern but insufficient evidence showed minimal impairment of rights under s.1.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal also agreed ... the Attorney General had not provided sufficient evidence that it impaired the respondents’ rights as little as possible

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found insufficient evidence to justify rights impairment under s.1 despite pressing legislative purpose.

propositions.text: Retrospective application of s.10(1) AEPA violates s.11(h) right not to be punished again.
propositions.quote: The respondents submit that the retrospective application provision, s. 10(1) of the AEPA , violates their right under s. 11 (h) of the Charter not to be “punished . . . again”

propositions.text: Punishment should be broadly read beyond duplication of proceedings.
propositions.quote: They urge a broad reading of the term “punishment” that is not limited to the duplication of criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings.

propositions.text: Retrospective repeal eliminating early day parole eligibility was punitive in effect and purpose.
propositions.quote: the retrospective application of the repeal ... was punitive in its effect. The respondents also argue ... that it was punitive in its purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The respondents argue s.10(1) AEPA's retrospective repeal violates s.11(h) by punitive effect and purpose, urging broad 'punishment' reading.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) should be narrowly read to exclude elimination of early day parole eligibility as punishment.
propositions.quote: The Crown urges a narrow, textual reading of s. 11 (h) that would exclude the elimination of early day parole eligibility from the definition of “punishment”.

propositions.text: Retrospective repeal aims at rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety, not punishment; effect reflects this.
propositions.quote: It argues that the retrospective application of the repeal was adopted in furtherance of the goals of rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety and confidence in the administration of justice, not that of punishment.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) not engaged without duplication of criminal proceedings.
propositions.quote: In this Court, the Crown further argues that s. 11 (h) is not engaged, because being “punished . . . again” requires a duplication of proceedings that are criminal in nature

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues s.11(h) excludes early day parole elimination as punishment and requires duplication of criminal proceedings.

propositions.text: Will first consider if s.11(h) applies absent duplication, then scope of punishment, then if provision is punishment in purpose or effect.
propositions.quote: I will begin with this last question of whether s. 11 (h) applies absent a duplication of proceedings. I will then consider the scope of the “punishment” concept ...

paragraphs.summary: The court outlines its approach: consider s.11(h) applicability without duplication, then punishment scope, then if provision is punishment.

propositions.text: Trial court and Court of Appeal did not address if s.11(h) applies without duplication of proceedings.
propositions.quote: Neither the trial court nor the Court of Appeal dealt with this question.

propositions.text: Both courts agreed s.11(h) protects against double jeopardy defined as not being tried or punished again for same offence.
propositions.quote: The two courts agreed that s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, which Levine J.A. defined as protection “from being tried or punished again for an offence for which the offender has already been found guilty and punished”

paragraphs.summary: The court notes earlier courts did not address s.11(h) without duplication; both agreed s.11(h) protects against double jeopardy.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) states right not to be tried or punished again if finally found guilty and punished.
propositions.quote: Section 11 (h) of the Charter reads as follows: 11. Any person charged with an offence has the right ... (h) if finally acquitted ... not to be tried for it again and, if finally found guilty and punished for the offence, not to be tried or punished for it again;

paragraphs.summary: The court quotes s.11(h) stating the right not to be tried or punished again if finally found guilty and punished.

propositions.text: Parliament enacted s.11(h) to protect against double jeopardy, mirroring ICCPR art.14.7.
propositions.quote: Parliament’s purpose in enacting s. 11 (h) was to protect against double jeopardy. Section 11 (h) mirrors ... art. 14.7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights

propositions.text: ICCPR art.14.7 prohibits being tried or punished again for an offence already finally convicted or acquitted.
propositions.quote: 7. No one shall be liable to be tried or punished again for an offence for which he has already been finally convicted or acquitted

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.11(h) protects against double jeopardy, mirroring ICCPR article 14.7 prohibiting retrial or punishment.

propositions.text: Definition of double jeopardy is contested and complex, involving protection against multiple trials and punishments.
propositions.quote: But equating s. 11 (h) with double jeopardy does not conclude the discussion ... The subject is one of the utmost complexity and subtlety ... protection against harassment of multiple trials ... and multiple punishment.

propositions.text: Concern about double punishment is based on fairness of proportionate punishment.
propositions.quote: The concern to do something about double punishment stems from a distinct consideration based far more squarely on the fairness of proportionate punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites academic commentary that double jeopardy is complex, covering multiple trials and punishments, based on fairness.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) has narrow scope and limited impact on double jeopardy and double punishment protection.
propositions.quote: the scope of s. 11 (h) is narrow ... s. 11 (h) has had “little impact on the protection of the accused against double jeopardy and double punishment”

propositions.text: Broader double jeopardy interpretations may fit better under s.7 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: broader interpretations of double jeopardy may fit more easily into s. 7 of the Charter

propositions.text: Sections 11(g) and 11(i) explicitly address retrospectivity and harsher punishment after crime commission.
propositions.quote: there are two provisions that deal explicitly with retrospectivity: s. 11 (g) ... and s. 11 (i) ...

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s.11(h) is narrow, broader double jeopardy fits s.7, and s.11(g) and (i) address retrospectivity.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) applies to protect against being punished again even without a second proceeding.
propositions.quote: the language of s. 11 (h), the academic literature and this Court’s jurisprudence support a reading ... applies where an offender has been sentenced, even if no separate proceeding has taken place.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s.11(h) protects against being punished again even absent a second proceeding.

propositions.text: Plain meaning of s.11(h) shows protection against being tried or punished again is independent and sufficient to engage s.11(h).
propositions.quote: The disjunctive language of the words “tried or punished” clearly indicates that s. 11 (h)’s protection against additional punishment is independent of its protection against being tried again.

propositions.text: Conjunctive language “found guilty and punished” emphasizes disjunctive “tried or punished”.
propositions.quote: The conjunctive language of the words “found guilty and punished” further accentuates the disjunctive language of “tried or punished”.

propositions.text: Protection applies to harassment of multiple trials and additional punishment.
propositions.quote: as Stuart notes in respect of double jeopardy more generally, the protection applies to both the harassment of multiple trials and the harassment of additional punishment

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s.11(h)'s plain meaning protects against being tried or punished again independently.

propositions.text: It is more questionable to punish without a proceeding than with one; s.11(h) protects against punishment without trial.
propositions.quote: It would be far more questionable to punish someone without a proceeding than to punish him or her with a proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: The court reasons s.11(h) protects against punishment without trial as more questionable than punishment with trial.

propositions.text: Narrow scope of s.11(h) does not preclude its application to double punishment without new proceeding.
propositions.quote: this does not preclude the application of s. 11 (h) to protect against double punishment where no new proceeding has taken place

propositions.text: Some authors focus on what constitutes a second proceeding for s.11(h), but this does not limit s.11(h) in double punishment cases without proceedings.
propositions.quote: While some authors focus on the fine points of what constitutes a second proceeding for the purposes of s. 11 (h) ... this does not limit the application of s. 11 (h) in cases of double punishment in which no such proceeding took place.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.11(h) applies to double punishment without new proceedings despite narrow scope and academic debate.

propositions.text: Early s.11(h) cases addressed double jeopardy from criminal and non-criminal proceedings, not punishment without second proceeding.
propositions.quote: The early cases with respect to s. 11 (h) concerned situations ... The question was whether the non-criminal proceeding or sanction triggered the protection against double jeopardy

propositions.text: McLachlin J. stated s.11(h) protects against duplication in criminal proceedings, not two different proceedings from same act.
propositions.quote: The Crown cites the following comment made by McLachlin J. ... “Section 11 (h) provides protection against duplication in proceedings of a criminal nature. It does not preclude two different proceedings, one criminal and the other not criminal, flowing from the same act”

propositions.text: McLachlin J.'s comment must be read in context of criminal nature inquiry; protection can be triggered by criminal or true penal consequences.
propositions.quote: this passage must be read in context ... Even in the early s. 11 (h) cases, it was found that the protection ... could be triggered by proceedings that are criminal in nature or by “true penal consequences”.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes early s.11(h) cases focused on criminal/non-criminal proceedings; McLachlin J.'s comment supports protection triggered by criminal or penal consequences.

propositions.text: Rodgers case held s. 11 applies only when a person is charged with an offence, and DNA order application does not engage s. 11
propositions.quote: the protection extended by s. 11 can only be invoked when “[a] person [is] charged with an offence”. Therefore, in and of itself, the application for a DNA order does not at all engage s. 11

propositions.text: Rodgers court rejected Crown's narrow construction of s. 11(h) limiting it to criminal proceedings duplication
propositions.quote: In Rodgers, the Court rejected the narrow construction of s. 11 (h) advanced by the Crown in the case at bar according to which it is limited to cases involving a duplication of proceedings that are criminal in nature

propositions.text: s. 11(h) protects against double punishment even without a second proceeding
propositions.quote: I find that s. 11 (h) does protect an offender who has been tried and sentenced against double punishment even in the absence of a second proceeding

propositions.text: Rodgers supports conclusion that s. 11(h) protects against double punishment without second proceeding
propositions.quote: Rodgers, a more recent case, supports my conclusion

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Rodgers supports that s. 11(h) protects against double punishment even without a second proceeding, rejecting Crown's narrow view.

propositions.text: Must determine if the situation here amounts to punishment under s. 11(h) after concluding s. 11(h) allows claims without second proceeding
propositions.quote: I must now determine whether the situation in the instant case amounts to punishment

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if the current case situation constitutes punishment under s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings trigger s. 11(h) protection against double jeopardy
propositions.quote: It has always been clear that criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings trigger the protection against double jeopardy

propositions.text: Second criminal or quasi-criminal charge for same act engages s. 11(h) even if consequence is slight
propositions.quote: Thus, a second criminal or quasi-criminal charge with respect to the same act engages s. 11 (h) even if the consequence is slight

paragraphs.summary: The court finds criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings trigger s. 11(h) protection, including second charges for same act.

propositions.text: Wigglesworth held s. 11(h) applies to non-criminal proceedings with true penal consequences
propositions.quote: Wigglesworth made it clear that the protection against double jeopardy may be triggered not only by proceedings that are criminal or quasi-criminal in nature, but also by non-criminal proceedings that result in a sanction with true penal consequences

propositions.text: True penal consequence means imprisonment or fine imposed to redress wrong to society, not internal discipline
propositions.quote: a true penal consequence which would attract the application of s. 11 is imprisonment or a fine which by its magnitude would appear to be imposed for the purpose of redressing the wrong done to society at large rather than to the maintenance of internal discipline within the limited sphere of activity

paragraphs.summary: Wigglesworth held s. 11(h) applies to non-criminal proceedings with true penal consequences like imprisonment or fines.

propositions.text: Wigglesworth found internal RCMP disciplinary proceeding involved true penal consequences due to possible imprisonment
propositions.quote: although the internal disciplinary proceeding against an RCMP officer was neither criminal nor quasi-criminal “in nature”, it was found to involve “true penal consequences” because the possible sanctions included imprisonment for up to one year

propositions.text: Shubley found internal prison disciplinary sanctions lacked true penal consequences as no fines or imprisonment involved
propositions.quote: a sanction imposed in an internal prison disciplinary proceeding — close confinement for a period of five days on a special diet — fell short of “true penal consequences”, in part because the possible sanctions involved neither fines nor imprisonment

paragraphs.summary: Wigglesworth found RCMP disciplinary sanctions true penal consequences; Shubley found prison disciplinary sanctions were not.

propositions.text: Rodgers revisited punishment definition, accepted imprisonment and heavy fines as true penal consequences but punishment not limited to these
propositions.quote: Charron J. accepted that imprisonment and heavy fines constitute “true penal consequences”, but reasoned that “punishment” is not limited to these two types of sanctions

propositions.text: Charron J. identified features of punitive sanctions less severe than imprisonment or heavy fines
propositions.quote: She set out to identify features characteristic of punitive sanctions that could be used to determine whether a given sanction that is less severe than imprisonment or a heavy fine nevertheless constitutes punishment

propositions.text: Examples of orders a sentencing court might make include forfeiture, firearm prohibition, driving prohibition, restitution
propositions.quote: She mentioned various orders a sentencing court might make, such as an order for forfeiture, a firearm prohibition, a driving prohibition or an order for restitution

paragraphs.summary: Rodgers expanded punishment definition beyond imprisonment and fines, identifying features of less severe punitive sanctions.

propositions.text: Rodgers two-part punishment test: sanction part of arsenal of sanctions for offence and imposed in furtherance of sentencing principles
propositions.quote: As a general rule, it seems to me that the consequence will constitute a punishment when it forms part of the arsenal of sanctions to which an accused may be liable in respect of a particular offence and the sanction is one imposed in furtherance of the purpose and principles of sentencing

propositions.text: DNA order not part of criminal sanctions arsenal, does not attach stigma, deterrent effect not punishment
propositions.quote: Charron J. found that a DNA order is no more a part of the arsenal of criminal sanctions than the taking of a photograph or fingerprints. It does not on its own attach a stigma to the offender, and while it may have a deterrent effect, not all deterrent measures can be characterized as punishment

propositions.text: Example: random traffic stops deter but are not punishment
propositions.quote: By way of example, Charron J. cites random traffic stops to check for alcohol consumption, which hopefully deter people from drinking and driving but are not punishment

paragraphs.summary: Rodgers test defines punishment as sanction part of criminal arsenal and imposed for sentencing; DNA order not punishment.

propositions.text: Current case pushes punishment concept limits, requiring revisiting s. 11(h) principles
propositions.quote: the case at bar once again pushes the limits of the “punishment” concept, requiring us to revisit the principles that define the scope of s. 11 (h)

propositions.text: Wigglesworth and Rodgers tests do not fully address current case question
propositions.quote: the question in the instant case eludes both tests

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the current case challenges the punishment concept and existing tests do not fully apply.

propositions.text: Must determine if retrospective parole eligibility changes that modify existing sanction manner constitute punishment
propositions.quote: this case requires us to determine whether retrospective changes to parole eligibility, which modify the manner in which an existing sanction is carried out, constitute punishment

propositions.text: Alleged punishment is not a second proceeding or sanction but frustration of offender's original punishment expectations
propositions.quote: The alleged punishment is neither a second proceeding nor a “sanction” in the sense contemplated in Rodgers. Rather, the offender’s expectations about the original punishment or sanction have been frustrated

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if retrospective parole changes frustrating offender's expectations constitute punishment.

propositions.text: Rodgers test's first branch defines punishment by traditional Criminal Code sanctions, equating sentence and sanction
propositions.quote: In the first branch of the Rodgers test, “punishment” is defined by referring to the traditional forms of punishment provided for in the Criminal Code , in which “[t]he words ‘sentence’ and ‘sanction’ are . . . used interchangeably”

propositions.text: Parole grant changes sentence conditions, not sentence itself (R. v. M. (C.A.))
propositions.quote: a grant of parole represents a change in the conditions under which a judicial sentence must be served, rather than a reduction of the judicial sentence itself

propositions.text: Changes to parole system generally not part of 'arsenal of sanctions' in Rodgers test
propositions.quote: changes to the parole system do not generally form part of the “arsenal of sanctions” contemplated in Rodgers

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Rodgers test excludes parole changes as they alter sentence conditions, not sentence itself.

propositions.text: Retrospective parole changes may extend incarceration, which is the most severe punishment
propositions.quote: a retrospective change to parole eligibility may have the effect of extending an offender’s term of incarceration. Incarceration is “the most severe deprivation of liberty known to our law”

propositions.text: Incarceration and heavy fines are benchmark punishments under Rodgers test
propositions.quote: Incarceration and heavy fines are the benchmark sanctions against which other, less severe sanctions are assessed under the Rodgers test

propositions.text: Incarceration as punishment is core assumption of Rodgers test
propositions.quote: That incarceration constitutes “punishment” is a core underlying assumption of the Rodgers test

paragraphs.summary: The court finds incarceration is the benchmark punishment and retrospective parole changes may extend incarceration.

propositions.text: Rodgers test is overly formalistic for parole changes, excluding most parole changes though they increase incarceration likelihood
propositions.quote: when applied in this context, the Rodgers test is overly formalistic, as the “arsenal of sanctions” test would exclude most changes to parole eligibility, whereas even marginal increases in the likelihood of additional incarceration easily meet the test

propositions.text: Rodgers test does not identify functional increases in punishment harshness from retrospective parole changes
propositions.quote: Rodgers test does not assist in identifying situations in which, from a functional rather than a formalistic perspective, the harshness of punishment has been increased

propositions.text: Rodgers test designed to assess discrete sanctions, not modifications to original sanctions
propositions.quote: Rodgers test was designed for a different purpose, namely to determine whether a discrete sanction — one that does not modify the original sanction — has the characteristics of a criminal sanction, and thus constitutes “punishment”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Rodgers test is formalistic and unsuitable for assessing retrospective parole changes as punishment.

propositions.text: Second branch of Rodgers test (sanction furthers sentencing principles) awkward for parole changes
propositions.quote: The second branch of the Rodgers test — whether the sanction furthers the purpose and principles of sentencing — is also an awkward fit in this situation

propositions.text: Rehabilitation and reintegration are sentencing and parole principles, so all retrospective parole changes could be said to further sentencing principles
propositions.quote: rehabilitation and reintegration are principles applied in parole administration, but they are also sentencing principles. It would seem that all retrospective changes to parole eligibility could therefore be said to further the purpose and principles of sentencing

propositions.text: Not all retrospective parole changes are punitive despite furthering sentencing principles
propositions.quote: it is clear to me that not all such changes would be punitive

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the second Rodgers test branch is awkward for parole changes, as not all are punitive despite furthering sentencing principles.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) precludes: (a) criminal/quasi-criminal retrial; (b) additional sanction meeting Rodgers test; (c) retrospective changes adding punishment
propositions.quote: s. 11(h) precludes the following further state actions in relation to the same offence: (a) a proceeding that is criminal or quasi-criminal in nature; (b) an additional sanction or consequence that meets the two-part Rodgers test; and (c) retrospective changes to the conditions of the original sanction which have the effect of adding to the offender’s punishment

propositions.text: Current case concerns third type: retrospective repeal altering parole expectations
propositions.quote: The case at bar concerns the third of these types of double punishment under s. 11(h). It is not the repeal of the APR provisions that is alleged to be unconstitutional, but the retrospective application of that repeal

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 11(h) forbids retrial, additional Rodgers-type sanctions, and retrospective punishment changes; this case concerns the last.

propositions.text: Charter s. 11(g) protects against retroactive criminal laws; s. 11(i) protects against increased punishment after crime commission
propositions.quote: s. 11 (g), which protects against retroactive criminal laws... Section 11 (i)... protects against increases in punishment between the time of commission of the crime and the time of sentencing

propositions.text: Peter Hogg states Canadian constitutional law lacks prohibition on retroactive laws except s. 11(g)
propositions.quote: [a]part from s. 11 (g), Canadian constitutional law contains no prohibition of retroactive (or ex post facto) laws

propositions.text: s. 11(g) and (i) express society's repudiation of retroactive punishment
propositions.quote: Both these provisions express society’s repudiation of retroactive punishment, broadly defined

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Charter s. 11(g) and (i) protect against retroactive criminal laws and increased punishment.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, not expressly retroactivity
propositions.quote: Section 11(h) is not expressly concerned with retroactivity. Its purpose is to protect against double jeopardy

propositions.text: Retrospective parole modifications may increase punishment and engage s. 11(h)
propositions.quote: Retrospective modification of the parole system after an offender was sentenced may have the effect of increasing the offender’s punishment, thereby engaging s. 11 (h)

propositions.text: Non-punitive legislative changes can become punitive if applied retrospectively
propositions.quote: A legislative change that is not in itself punitive can acquire a punitive character by being applied retrospectively

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, and retrospective parole changes may increase punishment.

propositions.text: Offenders have constitutionally protected expectations as to sentence duration, not conditions
propositions.quote: Generally speaking, offenders have constitutionally protected expectations as to the duration, but not the conditions, of their sentences

propositions.text: Not all parole management changes are punitive despite affecting liberty interest
propositions.quote: Various changes in the management of an offender’s parole are not punitive, even though they may engage the offender’s liberty interest

propositions.text: Cunningham held Charter s. 7 protects only significant liberty limitations, not trivial ones
propositions.quote: The Charter does not protect against insignificant or “trivial” limitations of rights

propositions.text: Substantial change in conditions amounting to further deprivation of liberty required for s. 7 protection
propositions.quote: there must be a “substantial change in conditions amounting to a further deprivation of liberty”

paragraphs.summary: Cunningham held offenders have protected expectations on sentence duration, and s.7 protects only substantial liberty deprivations.

propositions.text: Substantial change requirement from s.7 context not imported into s.11(h) context
propositions.quote: The requirement of a “substantial change in conditions amounting to a further deprivation of liberty” was articulated in the context of s. 7 , and I will not import it into that of s. 11(h)

propositions.text: Retrospective parole changes engaging s.7 liberty interest may not be punishment under s.11(h)
propositions.quote: Retrospective changes to the parole system that engage a liberty interest under s. 7 will not necessarily constitute punishment for the purposes of s. 11(h)

propositions.text: Offender has liberty expectation based on parole system at sentencing; thwarting it may engage s.7 liberty interest
propositions.quote: the Court recognized that an offender has an expectation of liberty that is based on the parole system in place at the time of his or her sentencing, and that thwarting that expectation may engage a constitutionally protected liberty interest

propositions.text: Cunningham: more liberty on mandatory supervision than in prison
propositions.quote: One has ‘more’ liberty, or a better quality of liberty, when one is serving time on mandatory supervision than when one is serving time in prison

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.7's substantial change test not imported to s.11(h); parole expectations may engage s.7 liberty interest.

propositions.text: Not all parole liberty expectations are constitutionally protected
propositions.quote: not all expectations of liberty in the parole context are constitutionally protected

propositions.text: Some retrospective parole changes may be new punishment under s.11(h), others not
propositions.quote: Some retrospective changes to the parole system affect the expectation of liberty of an offender who has already been sentenced to such an extent that they amount to new punishment, while other changes have a more limited impact and do not trigger Charter protection

paragraphs.summary: The court finds some retrospective parole changes constitute new punishment under s.11(h), others do not.

propositions.text: No universal formula for retrospective parole changes; context-specific
propositions.quote: I will not articulate a formula that would apply to every case, because such a formula is not needed to resolve this appeal and the effect of every retrospective change will be context-specific

propositions.text: Dominant consideration is extent offender's settled liberty expectation is thwarted by retrospective legislative action
propositions.quote: the dominant consideration in each case will in my view be the extent to which an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted by retrospective legislative action

propositions.text: Retrospective frustration of liberty expectation constitutes punishment
propositions.quote: It is the retrospective frustration of an expectation of liberty that constitutes punishment

propositions.text: Retrospective parole eligibility change automatically lengthening incarceration is clear double punishment under s.11(h)
propositions.quote: a retrospective change to the rules governing parole eligibility that has the effect of automatically lengthening the offender’s period of incarceration constitutes additional punishment contrary to s. 11 (h) of the Charter

paragraphs.summary: The court finds punishment is retrospective frustration of liberty expectation; automatic incarceration lengthening is clear double punishment.

propositions.text: Sentencing judges may consider delayed parole eligibility as part of the sentence under the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: the punitive effect of delayed parole eligibility is expressly recognized in the Criminal Code , which empowers a sentencing judge to consider delayed parole eligibility to be part of the sentence in certain circumstances.

propositions.text: Sentencing judges should not consider parole eligibility in assessing sentence fitness (Zinck).
propositions.quote: a sentencing judge is not to consider parole eligibility in assessing the fitness of the sentence (Zinck, at para. 18)

propositions.text: Section 743.6(1) allows courts to impose delayed parole eligibility for denunciation or deterrence.
propositions.quote: s. 743.6(1) empowers a court to impose delayed parole eligibility for the purpose of denunciation or of specific or general deterrence.

propositions.text: Sentencing judges may increase parole ineligibility for second degree murder (Chaisson).
propositions.quote: a sentencing judge may increase the parole ineligibility period of an offender convicted of second degree murder (Chaisson, at para. 12).

propositions.text: Sentencing courts determine fixed parole ineligibility terms in murder cases (R. v. Wust).
propositions.quote: In murder cases, the sentencing court will determine a fixed term of parole ineligibility: s. 745.4 of the Code.

propositions.text: Parole ineligibility duration is part of punishment and sentencing policy (Shropshire).
propositions.quote: the duration of parole ineligibility is the only difference in terms of punishment between first and second degree murder, which “clearly indicates that parole ineligibility is part of the ‘punishment’ and thereby forms an important element of sentencing policy” (para. 23).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds sentencing judges may consider delayed parole eligibility as part of the sentence, citing Criminal Code and case law recognizing parole ineligibility as punishment.

propositions.text: Retrospective imposition of delayed parole eligibility constitutes punishment triggering s. 11(h) protection against double punishment.
propositions.quote: retrospectively imposing delayed parole eligibility on offenders who have already been sentenced constitutes punishment. Where Parliament imposes through retrospective legislation a consequence that sentencing judges may themselves impose for the purpose of punishment, the s. 11 (h) protection against double punishment applies.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes retrospective delayed parole eligibility is punishment and triggers s. 11(h) protection against double punishment.

propositions.text: Whether less drastic retrospective parole changes constitute double punishment depends on case circumstances.
propositions.quote: Whether less drastic retrospective changes to parole constitute double punishment will depend on the circumstances of the particular case.

propositions.text: Retrospective changes not substantially increasing incarceration risk are generally not punitive.
propositions.quote: Generally speaking, a retrospective change to the conditions of a sentence will not be considered punitive if it does not substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration.

propositions.text: Indicators of lower incarceration risk include individualized decision making and procedural rights.
propositions.quote: Indicators of a lower risk of additional incarceration include a process in which individualized decision making focused on the offender’s circumstances continues to prevail and procedural rights continue to be guaranteed in the determination of parole eligibility.

propositions.text: Discretionary release with procedural safeguards was constitutional in Cunningham.
propositions.quote: the replacement of an automatic release system with a discretionary release system was found to be constitutional in Cunningham owing in part to various procedural safeguards, including a hearing and the entitlement to counsel.

propositions.text: Presence of procedural safeguards is relevant to likelihood of increased punishment severity under s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: While s. 11(h) is not directly concerned with procedural safeguards, the presence or absence of such safeguards is relevant in considering the likelihood of the punishment’s severity being increased.

propositions.text: Dominant consideration is the extent to which offender’s settled liberty expectation is thwarted.
propositions.quote: the dominant consideration will be the extent to which the offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted.

propositions.text: Changes extending incarceration without regard to individual circumstances and procedural safeguards violate s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: A change that directly results in an extension of the period of incarceration without regard to the offender’s individual circumstances and without procedural safeguards in the assessment process will clearly violate s. 11(h).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that less drastic retrospective parole changes may not be punitive if individualized decision making and safeguards remain, but changes extending incarceration without safeguards violate s. 11(h).

propositions.text: A law may violate the Charter in its purpose or effect; failing purpose test ends inquiry.
propositions.quote: A law may violate the Charter in its purpose or in its effect: “If the legislation fails the purpose test, there is no need to consider further its effects, since it has already been demonstrated to be invalid” (R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, at p. 334).

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal considered purpose first, then effect of s. 10(1) of AEPA.
propositions.quote: both the trial judge and the Court of Appeal considered the purpose of the law first, followed by its effect.

propositions.text: Trial judge held s. 10(1) violates Charter in purpose and effect; Court of Appeal ruled only on effect.
propositions.quote: The trial judge held that s. 10(1) of the AEPA violates the Charter in both its purpose and its effect, whereas the Court of Appeal declined, because the effect of s. 10(1) renders it unconstitutional, to rule on the constitutionality of its purpose.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Court of Appeal that s. 10(1) violates Charter in its effect, for different reasons.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Court of Appeal, but for different reasons, that s. 10(1) violates the Charter in its effect.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that laws may violate Charter in purpose or effect; agrees with Court of Appeal that s. 10(1) violates Charter in effect.

propositions.text: Overall purpose of AEPA is not disputed and is constitutionally valid.
propositions.quote: First of all, the overall purpose of the AEPA is not at issue. I agree with the Court of Appeal, which found that there is no serious dispute about the validity of that purpose

propositions.text: Respondents take no issue with AEPA's purpose to enhance parole regimes and public safety.
propositions.quote: the respondents take no issue with the AEPA on that basis.

propositions.text: Respondents dispute Parliament's decision to apply repeal retrospectively to already sentenced offenders.
propositions.quote: What is at issue is Parliament’s decision to make the repeal apply retrospectively, by means of s. 10(1) of the AEPA , to offenders who had already been sentenced.

propositions.text: Issue is the purpose of retrospective application of s. 10(1) of AEPA.
propositions.quote: What is the purpose of this retrospective application?

paragraphs.summary: The court finds AEPA's overall purpose undisputed; the issue is the purpose of its retrospective application under s. 10(1).

propositions.text: Retrospective parole eligibility changes violate s. 11(h) if purpose is to prolong incarceration.
propositions.quote: where legislation makes retrospective changes to parole eligibility, it will violate s. 11 (h) if its purpose is to prolong the offender’s period of incarceration.

propositions.text: Crown says retrospective repeal furthers rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety, and confidence goals.
propositions.quote: The Crown submits that Parliament’s decision to have the repeal apply retrospectively was made in furtherance of the goals of rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety and confidence in the administration of justice.

propositions.text: Crown argues retrospective repeal applies immediately and uniformly to all offenders, including sentenced ones.
propositions.quote: These goals were better served by having the repeal apply “immediately and uniformly to all offenders, including those already sentenced but not yet released” (A.F., at para. 84).

propositions.text: Respondents and trial judge argue retrospective application aims at denunciation, deterrence, and punishment.
propositions.quote: Both they and Holmes J. have cited Hansard to show that retrospective application was meant to serve the purposes of denunciation, deterrence and punishment.

propositions.text: Central question: Did Parliament intend to lengthen incarceration time for already sentenced offenders?
propositions.quote: Was Parliament’s purpose to lengthen the time to be served in jail by offenders who had already been sentenced?

paragraphs.summary: The court states retrospective parole changes violate s. 11(h) if intended to prolong incarceration; Crown argues legitimate goals, respondents allege punitive purpose.

propositions.text: MP said non-retroactivity would deny justice to victims of notorious crimes.
propositions.quote: one Member of Parliament had said that if the repeal was not retroactive, the victims of a notorious crime committed before the repeal “will never have any kind of justice served”

propositions.text: This suggests Parliament intended to extend incarceration for already sentenced offenders, conflicting with s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: This strongly suggests that Parliament intended to extend the period of incarceration of offenders who had already been sentenced, which would mean that the purpose of the provision was incompatible with s. 11 (h).

paragraphs.summary: An MP's statement suggests Parliament intended to extend incarceration for already sentenced offenders, conflicting with s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Despite troubling Hansard passages, court accepts Crown's articulation of Parliament's purpose as legitimate parole objectives.
propositions.quote: Despite some troubling passages from Hansard that are suggestive of an unconstitutional purpose, I accept the Crown’s articulation of Parliament’s purpose for the following reasons.

propositions.text: Parole administration is distinct from sentencing; applying parole objectives universally is not prima facie unconstitutional.
propositions.quote: Parole administration is distinct from sentencing. Parliament... considered it desirable to pursue the objectives underlying those rules in respect of all offenders, including those who had already been sentenced. In light of the formal distinction... I see nothing prima facie unconstitutional about the purpose of applying legitimate parole objectives universally to all offenders.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts Crown's view that Parliament's purpose was legitimate parole objectives applied universally, distinct from sentencing.

propositions.text: Parliament's authority to modify sentence conditions is limited when effect constitutes punishment.
propositions.quote: Parliament’s authority to modify the conditions of an existing sentence... is limited where the effect of a modification is such that it constitutes punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Parliament's authority to modify sentence conditions is limited if the effect constitutes punishment.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) of AEPA deprived respondents of early day parole consideration, lengthening incarceration.
propositions.quote: The effect of the retrospective application provision, s. 10(1) of the AEPA , was to deprive the three respondents of the possibility of being considered for early day parole, which was an expectation they had had at the time they were sentenced.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 10(1) deprived respondents of early day parole consideration, lengthening incarceration.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) punished respondents again by imposing retrospective delay in day parole eligibility.
propositions.quote: In my view, s. 10(1) had the effect of punishing the respondents again. It retrospectively imposed a delay in day parole eligibility in relation to offences for which they had already been tried and punished.

propositions.text: The extended incarceration effect was automatic and ignored individual circumstances.
propositions.quote: The effect — extended incarceration — was automatic and without regard to individual circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 10(1) punished respondents again by automatically extending incarceration without regard to individual circumstances.

propositions.text: This case is a clear example of retrospective parole delay as punishment triggering s. 11(h) protection.
propositions.quote: This situation is one of the “clearest of cases” discussed above. The imposition of a delay in parole eligibility in this case is analogous to the imposition of delayed parole eligibility by a judge under the Criminal Code as part of the sentence.

propositions.text: Parole ineligibility is part of punishment (Shropshire).
propositions.quote: Iacobucci J. noted in Shropshire that the imposition of such a delay “clearly indicates that parole ineligibility is part of the ‘punishment’” (para. 23).

propositions.text: Retrospective legislation imposing parole delay triggers s. 11(h) protection against double punishment.
propositions.quote: Imposing this same consequence by means of retrospective legislation triggers the protection against double punishment set out in s. 11 (h).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds retrospective parole delay is punishment triggering s. 11(h) protection against double punishment.

propositions.text: Formal distinction between sentencing and parole administration does not shield retrospective parole delay from s. 11(h) scrutiny.
propositions.quote: My conclusion is not altered by the fact that the extension of parole ineligibility was imposed by means of legislation in the context of the CCRA , which concerns, inter alia, sentence administration, as opposed to being judicially imposed under the Criminal Code . This formal distinction does not change the basic point...

propositions.text: Retrospective parole delay thwarts offenders' liberty expectations and results in harsher penalties than at sentencing.
propositions.quote: the new period of parole ineligibility thwarted the expectations of liberty of offenders who had already been “tried or punished” for their offences and resulted in harsher penalties than they would have received under the legislation that was in force at the time of their sentencing.

propositions.text: Parliament cannot avoid s. 11(h) scrutiny by amending CCRA instead of Criminal Code to impose punishment.
propositions.quote: If that were the case, Parliament could enact punitive laws resulting in double punishment simply by choosing to amend the CCRA rather than the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that the formal distinction between sentencing and parole administration does not shield retrospective parole delay from s. 11(h) scrutiny.

propositions.text: Constitutionality of other APR abolition aspects was not seriously argued and requires full record for ruling.
propositions.quote: I would note that the constitutionality of other aspects of the abolition of APR was not seriously argued. Without a full record, I am not in a position to rule on the effect of changes to the review process...

propositions.text: Retrospective changes must be analyzed in detail for punitive effect; greater impact on liberty expectation increases s. 11(h) violation likelihood.
propositions.quote: every retrospective change must be analyzed in detail before conclusions can be drawn as to its possible punitive effect. The greater the impact on the offender’s settled expectation of liberty, or the greater the likelihood of additional incarceration, the more likely it is that a given retrospective change will violate s. 11 (h).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes other APR abolition aspects were not argued; retrospective changes require detailed analysis for punitive effect under s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Respondents argue s. 10(1) violates s. 7 by depriving liberty against fundamental justice principles.
propositions.quote: The respondents argue, in the alternative, that s. 10(1) violates s. 7 of the Charter by depriving the offender of liberty in contravention of the principles of fundamental justice.

propositions.text: Fundamental justice requires accused be tried and punished under law in force at offence time (R. v. Gamble).
propositions.quote: It is fundamental to any legal system which recognizes “the rule of law”... that an accused must be tried and punished under the law in force at the time the offence is committed.

propositions.text: Having found s. 11(h) violation, court finds s. 7 decision unnecessary.
propositions.quote: Having already found that the impugned provision offends s. 11 (h) of the Charter , I find it unnecessary to decide on the application of s. 7 .

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue s. 10(1) violates s. 7; court finds s. 11(h) violation makes s. 7 decision unnecessary.

propositions.text: Court prefers dealing with specific Charter guarantees over s. 7 when both pleaded (R. v. Harrer).
propositions.quote: When both s. 7 and a specific guarantee under the Charter are pleaded, this Court has generally shown a preference for dealing with the specific guarantee: R. v. Harrer...

propositions.text: Legal rights under ss. 8-14 are specific instances of fairness under s. 7 (R. v. Généreux).
propositions.quote: ss. 8 to 14 of the Charter , the “legal rights”, are specific instances of the basic tenets of fairness... entrenched as a constitutional minimum standard by s. 7 .

propositions.text: s. 7 offers no greater protection than specific s. 11 guarantees in some cases (R. v. Généreux, Pearson).
propositions.quote: s. 7 does not offer greater protection than the highly specific guarantee under s. 11 (d)... In R. v. Pearson... this Court applied the same reasoning in the context of a s. 11 (e) claim.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) specifically protects against retrospective parole delay punishment; court declines s. 7 arguments.
propositions.quote: Section 11 (h) protects against the specific infringement alleged in the case at bar: the retrospective legislative imposition of delayed parole eligibility, which has the effect of punishing the offender anew. I therefore decline to address the arguments with respect to s. 7 .

paragraphs.summary: The court explains preference for specific Charter guarantees; declines to address s. 7 as s. 11(h) specifically protects against retrospective parole delay punishment.

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal found s. 10(1) objectives pressing and substantial but failed minimal impairment.
propositions.quote: The trial judge held, and the Court of Appeal agreed, that the objectives of s. 10(1) of the AEPA are pressing and substantial, but they both found that the provision failed at the minimal impairment stage.

propositions.text: Court agrees with trial judge and Court of Appeal on minimal impairment failure.
propositions.quote: I agree with this result.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with trial judge and Court of Appeal that s. 10(1) fails minimal impairment despite pressing objectives.

propositions.text: Parliament based APR abolition on evidence that system was ineffective.
propositions.quote: Parliament based its decision to abolish APR on considerable evidence, presented by the Crown in this case, that the system was not working effectively.

propositions.text: Trial judge found ensuring sentences as administered reflect court sentences is pressing and substantial objective.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that the objective of ensuring that sentences as administered are consistent with the sentences courts impose... is pressing and substantial (para. 121).

propositions.text: Parliament's decision to apply objectives to all offenders reflects legitimate concern for uniformity and confidence.
propositions.quote: Parliament’s decision to apply these same objectives to all offenders... reflects its legitimate concern to ensure uniformity of parole administration and maintain confidence in the justice system.

propositions.text: Legislative measure including retrospective application is rationally connected to objectives.
propositions.quote: Having agreed that these objectives are pressing and substantial, I also find that the legislative measure — the AEPA — chosen by Parliament, including the retrospective application of its provisions, is rationally connected to the objectives.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament's objectives pressing and substantial and the AEPA's retrospective application rationally connected to them.

propositions.text: Crown failed to prove no less intrusive alternative to retrospective application existed.
propositions.quote: the Crown has not discharged its burden of proving that there was no less intrusive alternative to retrospective application of the AEPA ’s provisions.

propositions.text: Uniformity is worthy but no compelling evidence that APR continuation for sentenced offenders impairs it.
propositions.quote: Uniformity of parole administration may be a worthy objective, but the Crown has failed to provide compelling evidence that that uniformity would be impaired if the APR system continued to apply to offenders who were sentenced under it.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal concluded sentence management objectives do not justify depriving respondents of constitutional rights.
propositions.quote: Sentence management objectives in general, and the objectives of the AEPA in particular, are recognizably important, but they do not rise to such significance that justifies implementing them in a manner that deprives the respondents of their constitutional rights.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown failed to prove no less intrusive alternative to retrospective application; Court of Appeal concluded objectives don't justify constitutional rights deprivation.

propositions.text: Prospective repeal was available alternative to achieve objectives without violating s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: In my view, having the repeal apply only prospectively was an alternative means available to Parliament that would have enabled it to attain the objectives... without violating the s. 11 (h) rights of offenders who had already been sentenced.

propositions.text: Retrospective application damages confidence in justice system; no evidence prospective repeal would undermine objectives.
propositions.quote: the enactment of Charter -infringing legislation does great damage to that confidence. The Crown has produced no evidence to show why the alternative of a prospective repeal... would have significantly undermined its objectives.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds prospective repeal was a viable alternative that would not violate s. 11(h) and that retrospective application damages confidence without evidence prospective repeal would undermine objectives.

propositions.text: The remedy was overly broad as s. 10(1) was declared invalid entirely, but only delay in day parole eligibility infringed rights.
propositions.quote: The Crown argues in this Court that the remedy ordered by the summary trial judge and subsequently upheld by the Court of Appeal was overly broad, because she declared s. 10(1) to be invalid in its entirety, whereas only the delay in day parole eligibility — one consequence of the retroactive application of the repeal — had been found to infringe the respondents’ rights.

propositions.text: Offenders should benefit only from early day parole eligibility, not all abolished APR system aspects.
propositions.quote: The Crown submits that the offenders should benefit not from all aspects of the abolished APR system, including automatic referral to the Board, a review conducted on paper and more favourable release criteria, but only from the one aspect — early day parole eligibility — whose elimination has been found to be unconstitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues the remedy was overly broad, invalidating all of s. 10(1) though only delay in day parole eligibility infringed rights, and offenders should benefit only from early day parole eligibility.

propositions.text: Both courts held retrospective elimination of early day parole eligibility unconstitutional.
propositions.quote: Both of the courts below held that the retrospective application of the elimination of early day parole eligibility was unconstitutional.

propositions.text: No serious analysis was done on constitutionality of eliminating other APR system aspects retrospectively.
propositions.quote: No serious analysis was conducted into the constitutionality of the retrospective application of the elimination of other aspects of the APR system.

propositions.text: Punishment identified was delayed day parole eligibility, not changes to review procedure or release criteria.
propositions.quote: The “punishment” identified by the summary trial judge and upheld by the Court of Appeal was the delayed date for day parole eligibility, not the changes to the review procedure or to the criteria for release.

paragraphs.summary: The courts below found only the retrospective elimination of early day parole eligibility unconstitutional, identifying delayed day parole eligibility as punishment, not other APR changes.

propositions.text: Retrospective modification of review procedure and release criteria resembles accepted sentence management changes in Cunningham.
propositions.quote: the retrospective modification of the review procedure and the release criteria would seem to me to resemble the change relating to sentence management that this Court accepted in Cunningham.

propositions.text: Changes in how a sentence is served, favourable or unfavourable, are not contrary to fundamental justice principles.
propositions.quote: A change in the form in which a sentence is served, whether it be favourable or unfavourable to the prisoner, is not, in itself, contrary to any principle of fundamental justice.

propositions.text: Correctional authorities may make appropriate changes in sentence serving conditions, including place, conditions, training, or treatment.
propositions.quote: our system of justice has always permitted correctional authorities to make appropriate changes in how a sentence is served, whether the changes relate to place, conditions, training facilities, or treatment.

propositions.text: Legislative imposition of delayed day parole eligibility prolongs incarceration and constitutes punishment under s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: I have held that the legislative imposition of delayed day parole eligibility, by effectively prolonging the minimum period of incarceration of offenders who had already been sentenced, constitutes “punishment” for the purposes of s. 11 (h).

propositions.text: No other AEPA aspects found unconstitutional; pre-APR parole procedures can apply with early day parole timelines.
propositions.quote: I have not found other aspects of the AEPA to be unconstitutional. At first blush, I do not see anything impractical or offensive about having the pre-APR parole procedures that are now in force apply while at the same time following the timelines for early day parole eligibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds retrospective changes to review and release resemble accepted sentence management changes; delayed day parole eligibility is punishment under s.11(h), but other AEPA aspects are constitutional.

propositions.text: Courts below did not receive submissions on limited declaration now proposed; caution is needed before departing from prior remedy.
propositions.quote: the courts below did not receive submissions on the limited declaration now being proposed in this Court. This Court must exercise caution in deciding whether to depart from the remedy crafted by the trial judge and upheld by the Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: Cautious approach favours upholding full declaration of invalidity for two reasons.
propositions.quote: In my view, this cautious approach favours upholding the full declaration of invalidity. I draw this conclusion for two reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no prior submissions on the limited declaration and concludes caution favours upholding full invalidity declaration for two reasons.

propositions.text: Severance test asks if valid part is so bound to invalid part it cannot survive independently (Schachter v. Canada).
propositions.quote: The test for severance is whether the constitutionally sound portion of the scheme is so inextricably bound up with the part declared invalid that what remains cannot independently survive (Schachter v. Canada, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 679, at p. 697).

propositions.text: Doubts exist about respondents' claim that early day parole was functionally bound to APR scheme.
propositions.quote: I harbour doubts about the respondents’ submission that early day parole was functionally bound up with the rest of the APR scheme.

propositions.text: Without evidence on early day parole working with normal parole, court cannot presume Parliament would enact early day parole alone.
propositions.quote: to conclude that it was not in the absence of evidence on how early day parole would work in combination with normal parole procedures would be to overstep my judicial role. I cannot presume that Parliament would have enacted the legislation establishing early day parole on its own.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains severance test, doubts early day parole is bound to APR, and cannot presume Parliament would enact early day parole alone without evidence.

propositions.text: Even if early day parole could stand alone, severance is unworkable here due to legislative dependencies.
propositions.quote: even if it were clear that early day parole eligibility could stand, functionally, on its own, severance would not be workable in the context of this legislation.

propositions.text: Section 119.1 depends on ss. 125 and 126, which define eligibility and terms for accelerated parole review.
propositions.quote: Section 119.1 , which established the earlier eligibility period for day parole, was expressly dependent on both s. 125 , which defined the class of offenders who were automatically eligible for accelerated parole review, and s. 126, which set out the procedural and substantive terms for release on parole.

propositions.text: Section 119.1 sets earlier day parole eligibility period; s. 126.1 specifies ss. 125 and 126 apply to early day parole option.
propositions.quote: Section 119.1 read as follows: 119.1 The portion of the sentence of an offender who is eligible for accelerated parole review under sections 125 and 126 that must be served before the offender may be released on day parole is six months, or one sixth of the sentence, whichever is longer. Section 126.1 specified that ss. 125 and 126 applied to the early day parole option established by s. 119.1 .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds severance unworkable because s.119.1 depends on ss.125 and 126, which define eligibility and terms for accelerated parole review.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) of AEPA repealed ss. 125, 126, 126.1 retrospectively, withdrawing early day parole rights.
propositions.quote: Section 10(1) of the AEPA made the repeal of ss. 125 , 126 and 126.1 of the CCRA apply retrospectively and thus, in effect, withdrew the right to be considered for early day parole from offenders who had been eligible for such consideration prior to the enactment of the repeal provisions.

propositions.text: Section 119.1 cannot operate without ss. 125, 126, and 126.1 and is meaningless without them.
propositions.quote: The specific reference in s. 119.1 to “the sentence of an offender who is eligible for accelerated parole review under sections 125 and 126 ” means that this section cannot operate without ss. 125 , 126 and 126.1 and is thus meaningless without them.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.10(1) repealed ss.125-126.1 retrospectively, withdrawing early day parole rights, and s.119.1 is meaningless without those sections.

propositions.text: Reading s.10(1) to repeal ss.125-126.1 but not s.119.1 is impossible to implement.
propositions.quote: To read s. 10(1) of the AEPA down to make the repeal of ss. 125 to 126.1 apply retrospectively but not that of s. 119.1 , as the Crown proposes, would result in a provision that would be impossible to implement.

propositions.text: Therefore, declaration of invalidity of all of s.10(1) is upheld.
propositions.quote: I would therefore uphold the declaration of invalidity of all of s. 10(1) .

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes reading s.10(1) partially as Crown proposes is impossible, so it upholds invalidity of all s.10(1).

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed; s.10(1) of AEPA violates s.11(h) of Charter and is of no force or effect.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal and uphold the remedy ordered by the trial judge. Section 10(1) of the AEPA violates s. 11 (h) of the Charter and is accordingly of no force or effect.

propositions.text: Sections 125, 126, 126.1 and by implication 119.1 of CCRA continue to apply to offenders sentenced before AEPA's March 28, 2011 coming into force.
propositions.quote: Sections 125 , 126 , 126.1 and, by implication, 119.1 of the CCRA therefore continue to apply to offenders who were sentenced prior to the coming into force on March 28, 2011, of the AEPA . Appeal dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, finds s.10(1) violates s.11(h), and holds ss.125-126.1 and 119.1 continue to apply to pre-AEPA offenders.
